chapters.title: AI foundations and history
chapters.lede: The vocabulary and mental models that the rest of the manual depends on: what the different kinds of AI are, how we got to today's large language models, what those models actually compute, and when not to use one.

www.what: The map of the field: the nested relationship between AI, machine learning, deep learning and generative AI; the historical chain of ideas that led to transformers; and the basic units every LLM system is built from: tokens, parameters, embeddings and context.
www.why: Engineering decisions depend on these basics. If you know that an LLM predicts likely text rather than looking up facts, you design for hallucination from day one. If you know what a token is, you can estimate cost and latency before writing code.
www.where: Feasibility reviews, architecture proposals, cost estimates, and the first conversation with stakeholders about what AI can and cannot promise. Problem selection (1.6) decides whether a project should use an LLM at all.

chapters.title: Mathematics and the scientific computing toolkit
chapters.lede: The minimum mathematics needed to read model papers, debug training, and reason about retrieval and evaluation, plus the Python tools and hardware facts you will use every day.

www.what: Four branches of maths (linear algebra, probability, calculus, information theory) that describe how models represent data, learn and measure error; NumPy-style array programming; and how CPUs and GPUs execute that arithmetic.
www.why: Embeddings are vectors and similarity is a dot product. Training is gradient descent. The loss is cross-entropy. Evaluation needs confidence intervals. GPU memory planning is arithmetic on precision. You cannot reason about any of these without the vocabulary.
www.where: Vector search (cosine similarity), choosing a learning rate, reading a loss curve, deciding whether an A/B result is real, estimating whether a model fits in memory, and understanding why FP16 vs INT4 changes quality.

chapters.title: Machine learning fundamentals
chapters.lede: The discipline of learning from data: problem types, classic algorithms, data preparation, honest evaluation, and the failure modes (leakage, overfitting, drift) that also break LLM systems.

www.what: Methods that fit a function from examples so it generalises to new inputs, together with the practices that tell you whether it really does: data splits, metrics and error analysis.
www.why: LLM projects reuse every idea here. Evaluation sets are test splits. Prompt changes can overfit to a few examples. Judges and classifiers need precision/recall and calibration. Many enterprise problems are still best solved by a gradient-boosted tree, and you need to recognise them.
www.where: Fraud, churn and demand models; routing and triage classifiers; guardrail classifiers in front of LLMs; rerankers; quality scorers; and every offline evaluation and A/B test you run.

chapters.title: Deep learning fundamentals
chapters.lede: How neural networks compute, how they learn through backpropagation, what keeps training stable, and how PyTorch puts it all together. Transformers in chapter 5 are built from exactly these parts.

www.what: Neural networks: layers of simple units whose weights are learned by gradient descent. Plus the training machinery around them: losses, optimisers, schedules, normalisation and regularisation.
www.why: Every LLM is a deep network. Fine-tuning (chapter 13) is running a training loop. Reading a loss curve, choosing a learning rate for LoRA, and debugging NaNs all need this chapter. Embeddings, the basis of RAG, are learned representations.
www.where: Fine-tuning and evaluating models, training embedding models and rerankers, building small classifiers for guardrails, and understanding inference costs that come from network shape.

chapters.title: Transformers and LLM internals
chapters.lede: Open the box: how text becomes tokens, how attention lets every token use every other, what a transformer block contains, how generation and decoding work, and where the computational costs come from.

www.what: The transformer architecture that powers essentially every modern LLM and embedding model: tokenizer, embeddings, stacked attention and feed-forward blocks, and the decoding loop that turns probabilities into text.
www.why: Internals explain behaviour you will otherwise find mysterious: why costs grow with context length, why the same prompt gives different outputs, why some languages cost more, why models struggle to count letters, and what the KV cache in serving engines actually stores.
www.where: Choosing models and context sizes, setting temperature and stop sequences, estimating serving memory (14.1), choosing encoder vs decoder models for retrieval vs generation, and reading model cards and papers.

chapters.title: How models are trained
chapters.lede: The full life of a model: pretraining on trillions of tokens, curating that data, the arithmetic of scale, instruction tuning, preference optimisation and reinforcement learning, and how training is split across thousands of GPUs. The chapter ends with training a tiny language model yourself.

www.what: The pipeline that turns random weights into an assistant: self-supervised pretraining, then supervised fine-tuning on instructions, then optimisation against human or automatic preferences, all running on distributed hardware.
www.why: Training explains model behaviour: knowledge cutoffs, why chat formats must match exactly, why models are agreeable or verbose, why benchmark scores can be contaminated. It also tells you what customising a model really costs (chapter 13).
www.where: Reading model cards and licences, choosing between base and instruct models, preparing fine-tuning data in the right chat template, judging vendor claims, and estimating compute budgets.

chapters.title: Building applications with LLMs
chapters.lede: From an API call to a dependable feature: choosing models with evidence, writing and versioning prompts, assembling context, getting structured output and tool calls, managing conversation state, handling failure, and keeping business rules out of the model's hands.

www.what: The application layer around a model: prompt and context construction, output parsing and validation, tool integration, state, and the reliability engineering that wraps every model call.
www.why: Most production problems are not model problems. They are missing timeouts, unvalidated output, context that silently overflowed, retries that duplicated an action, or a policy decision left to a probabilistic model.
www.where: Every LLM feature: assistants, extraction pipelines, classification services, summarisation jobs, and as the core of RAG (9–10) and agents (11–12). Your first evaluation set (box at the end of 7.1) starts here.

chapters.title: Evaluation and experimentation
chapters.lede: How you know whether an AI system works, whether a change made it better, and whether it helps the business. Evaluation began with your first dataset in 7.1; this chapter builds the full practice, and later chapters add retrieval (9.7), scale (10.8), agent (11, 12.8) and production (17.9) evaluation on top.

www.what: Defining the task precisely, building representative test data, scoring outputs with code, people and model judges, quantifying uncertainty, and running offline experiments and online tests.
www.why: LLM outputs are open-ended and non-deterministic, so "it looked good in the demo" proves nothing. Every decision (model, prompt, chunk size, fine-tune, release) needs evidence. Without evaluation, you cannot improve safely or detect regressions.
www.where: Model selection, prompt changes, RAG tuning, fine-tuning release gates, CI quality gates (18.3), canary analysis (18.4), and turning production incidents into test cases (17.9).

chapters.title: Information retrieval and RAG fundamentals
chapters.lede: Retrieval-augmented generation connects a model to your organisation's knowledge. This chapter covers the full pipeline and the search techniques underneath it: keyword and vector search, approximate nearest neighbours, hybrid retrieval, reranking, query strategies, citations and retrieval metrics.

www.what: RAG retrieves relevant passages from a document collection at question time and places them in the model's context, so answers draw on current, private, citable sources rather than only on what the model memorised.
www.why: It is the most common enterprise LLM pattern. It addresses stale and missing knowledge and hallucination (1.5), supports access control and citations, and updates instantly when documents change, without retraining.
www.where: Internal knowledge assistants, customer support over help centres, policy and contract Q&A, engineering documentation search, sales enablement, and as the memory and research layer of agents.

chapters.title: RAG over millions of documents
chapters.lede: What changes when the corpus grows from a folder to tens of millions of documents across thousands of tenants: sizing, distributed ingestion, messy formats, continuous updates, sharding, permissions, migrations and realistic benchmarking.

www.what: The data-engineering and distributed-systems side of RAG: pipelines that ingest and keep millions of documents fresh, indexes split across machines, and access control enforced at retrieval time.
www.why: A prototype over 500 PDFs hides every hard problem. At scale, re-embedding costs real money, a single scanned-PDF format can break a pipeline, deletions must propagate for compliance, and one large tenant can overload a shard.
www.where: Enterprise search across SharePoint/Confluence/Drive, multi-tenant SaaS knowledge features, legal discovery, support knowledge across products, and research platforms over document archives.

chapters.title: Single-agent systems and durable workflows
chapters.lede: An agent is an LLM in a loop that chooses actions, calls tools and reacts to results. This chapter covers when autonomy is worth it, how the loop works, and the engineering that makes agents safe to run against real systems: tool contracts, permissions, memory, durable state, idempotency, human approval and the Model Context Protocol.

www.what: Systems where the model decides the sequence of steps at run time, plus the durable-execution techniques (state machines, checkpoints, idempotent actions, compensations) borrowed from distributed systems to make that safe.
www.why: Agents can complete multi-step tasks that fixed pipelines cannot, but they multiply every LLM risk: wrong actions have real side effects, loops burn money, and a prompt-injected document can trigger tool calls. Engineering discipline is what separates a demo from a dependable system.
www.where: Support agents that look up and modify orders, IT and DevOps assistants, research and analysis agents, coding agents, document-processing workflows with exceptions, and back-office automation with human sign-off.

chapters.title: Multi-agent architecture
chapters.lede: Systems in which several LLM-driven agents with different roles, tools or contexts cooperate. Multi-agent designs can raise quality on broad tasks, but they add cost, latency and new failure modes, so this chapter treats them as a distributed system to be justified by evaluation.

www.what: Architectures where work is split among agents: a coordinator delegating to workers, routers handing off to specialists, critics reviewing producers, all exchanging messages under explicit contracts.
www.why: Some tasks exceed one agent's context, toolset or focus. But every added agent is another probabilistic component; errors compound and costs multiply. Knowing the patterns and their failure modes lets you use them only where they pay off.
www.where: Deep research across many sources, large code changes, due-diligence reviews, incident investigation across systems, and customer journeys spanning departments with separate permissions.

chapters.title: Custom model adaptation for enterprise use
chapters.lede: A practical track for changing model behaviour with your own data: deciding whether to adapt at all, building datasets people trust, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, adapting embedding models and rerankers, measuring gains and regressions, and releasing models with the same rigour as software.

www.what: Fine-tuning, continued pretraining and distillation applied to enterprise problems, using the training mechanics from chapters 4 and 6, with the data and release processes needed to do it responsibly.
www.why: When prompting and retrieval plateau, adaptation can raise accuracy on narrow tasks, cut cost (a small tuned model replacing a large general one) and reduce latency. Done carelessly it silently breaks general abilities or safety, or memorises sensitive data.
www.where: High-volume extraction and classification, domain-specific language (legal, clinical, industrial), strict output formats, reliable tool calling for in-house APIs, and domain-tuned embeddings and rerankers for RAG.

chapters.title: Inference serving and GPU optimisation
chapters.lede: How models are served efficiently: where GPU memory goes, why prompt processing and token generation behave differently, the batching and caching techniques modern engines use, quantisation and speculative decoding, multi-GPU serving, autoscaling, and how to compare self-hosting with APIs. GPU-dependent behaviour is shown with simulations.

www.what: The systems engineering of running LLM inference: memory management, scheduling of many concurrent requests on accelerators, latency/throughput tuning, and capacity and cost planning.
www.why: Inference is where most of an AI product's cost and latency come from. Even if you use hosted APIs, these concepts explain rate limits, pricing for cached vs uncached tokens, time-to-first-token, and why long prompts are slow.
www.where: Self-hosting open models, choosing GPU types and counts, configuring vLLM/SGLang/TensorRT-LLM, setting SLOs for TTFT and token speed, autoscaling policies, and build-vs-buy decisions.

chapters.title: Architecture for millions of users
chapters.lede: Turning a working AI feature into a service that stays fast, available, fair and affordable under real-world load. It starts by converting user counts into the numbers that actually size infrastructure.

www.what: Capacity modelling, service-level objectives, workload separation, and the distributed-systems patterns (queues, caches, gateways, load shedding, circuit breakers, multi-region) applied to AI workloads with unusual properties: long, variable, expensive requests.
www.why: LLM requests last seconds, not milliseconds; cost scales with tokens; providers impose rate limits; GPUs are scarce and slow to add. Patterns that work for a CRUD API fail here unless adapted.
www.where: Consumer assistants, SaaS platforms embedding AI for thousands of tenants, internal copilots for large enterprises, and any system where AI traffic spikes (launches, business hours, incidents).

chapters.title: Enterprise security and governance
chapters.lede: AI systems add new attack surfaces (instructions hidden in data, models that can be talked into misusing tools) on top of every classic one. This chapter covers threat modelling, prompt injection and exfiltration, access control and sandboxing, tenant isolation, data protection, supply-chain risk, red teaming, incident response and the regulatory landscape.

www.what: The controls, processes and evidence that keep AI systems from leaking data, taking harmful actions, or violating law and policy, and that let an organisation demonstrate it.
www.why: An LLM cannot reliably tell instructions from data, so any text it reads can try to steer it. When it can also read private data and call tools, a single poisoned document can become a data breach. Security has to be designed into the architecture, not prompted in.
www.where: Architecture reviews, vendor and model selection, RAG and agent design, logging and retention policies, procurement and licensing, compliance audits, and the incident process when something goes wrong.

chapters.title: Observability, monitoring and production maintenance
chapters.lede: How to see what a running AI system is doing, detect when it degrades in speed, cost or quality, investigate incidents, and turn every production failure into a test that prevents its return.

www.what: Telemetry (logs, metrics, traces) across every component, AI-specific quality and cost signals, dashboards and alerts, on-call practice, and the feedback loop from production back to evaluation.
www.why: AI systems fail silently: an answer can be fluent, fast and wrong. Without traces you cannot tell whether retrieval or generation failed; without quality signals a regression can run for weeks; without cost attribution one tenant can double your bill unnoticed.
www.where: Every production deployment: on-call dashboards, incident investigations, cost reviews, quality reviews, capacity planning, compliance audits, and continuous improvement of prompts, retrieval and models.

chapters.title: MLOps, LLMOps and continuous delivery
chapters.lede: The release engineering that ties everything together: versioning every artefact that affects behaviour, reproducible infrastructure, automated gates, progressive rollouts with fast rollback, safe upgrades, feedback-driven improvement, and clear ownership.

www.what: MLOps applies DevOps practices to machine learning (data, training, models). LLMOps extends them to prompts, retrieval indexes, model providers, judges and agents. Together they form the delivery pipeline for AI behaviour.
www.why: An AI system's behaviour changes when any of code, prompt, model, data, index, configuration or provider changes, and several of those can change without a code deploy. Without discipline, nobody can say what is running, why quality changed, or how to roll back.
www.where: Every change to a production AI system: prompt edits, model upgrades, re-indexing, fine-tuned model releases, gateway routing changes, agent tool additions, and handing a system over to an operations team.
